                            Abstract                               1. Introduction
                                                                   Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [2–4, 17, 18, 22,
Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models reformulate             27, 28, 39, 40, 49, 56, 66] have recently enabled robot
vision-language models by tuning them with millions of             agents to perform complex manipulation tasks by fine-
robotic demonstrations. While they perform well when               tuning large vision-language models (VLMs) with millions
fine-tuned for a single embodiment or task family, extend-         of robotic demonstrations. By reformulating action learn-
ing them to multi-skill settings remains challenging: di-          ing as a language generation or policy decoding problem,
rectly merging VLA experts trained on different tasks re-          VLA models inherit broad visual grounding and seman-
sults in near-zero success rates. This raises a fundamen-          tic understanding from VLMs, and have shown notable

Figure 2. Overview of MergeVLA architecture. (1) To address destructive LoRA parameter interference in finetuned VLM, task masks
are applied to all merged LoRA modules to selectively activate the merged parameters contributing to task-relevant responses while sup-
pressing those that mislead other tasks. (2) To solve the incompatibility of action experts, the architecture is redesigned to contain only
cross-attention blocks and use sigmoid gate to preserve and rely on robust VLM features. Most blocks then can be merged except deeper
blocks named expert head are left unmerged due to their task specification. (3) To address the setting where the task identity is unknown at
inference time, a training-free test-time task router is adopted to dynamically select task-specified components by computing task relevance
from VLM hidden states in the value-based subspace of the merged action expert.

Impact of Mask Ratio. We analyze the effect of the task                a more reliable indicator of task identity.
mask under different λ, which controls the active ratio of the
mask. We vary λ from 0.2 to 0.9 and obtain the merged task             6. Conclusion
vector using Task Arithmetic (TA). Figure 6 (a) shows the              The lack of cross-skill capability in existing VLA mod-
active ratio of the mask across four tasks. As λ increases,            els remains a critical yet unexplored challenge. We show
fewer parameters remain active, with the LIBERO-Spatial                that current model merging techniques cannot be directly
task consistently showing the highest activation ratio, indi-          applied to VLAs due to destructive LoRA parameter inter-
cating its dominant weight contribution. We further eval-              ference and architectural incompatibility of action experts.
uate the impact of λ on the model’s performance in the                 We propose MergeVLA, a framework for merging VLA
LIBERO-Long task, as shown in Figure 6 (b). When λ                     models that is compatible with mainstream merging meth-
is small (e.g., 0.2), the mask activates too many parame-              ods toward an embodied generalist. Experiments across
ters, leading to severe task interference and even complete            three benchmarks demonstrate MergeVLA’s strong multi-
failure. In contrast, when λ lies between 0.6 and 0.9, the             task ability and robustness under distribution shifts, with
success rate exceeds 70%. These results suggest that mod-              transferability across embodiments. Future work will ex-
erate sparsity enables an effective balance between task-              plore this promising direction further, including whether
specific and merged task vectors. When the parameter dif-              larger VLM backbones remain compatible with our frame-
ferences across tasks are large, relying more on the pre-              work and whether pretraining on diverse robot datasets can
trained model yields better results, whereas emphasizing the           further enhance merging effectiveness.
